unit.title: Consult with clients and diagnose hair and scalp conditions

summary: This unit teaches you to talk with a client, find out what she wants and what her hair has been through, and then examine and test her hair and scalp so that you can choose a safe, suitable service. You will learn how a hair is built and how it grows, how to recognise the common hair and scalp conditions, which ones stop a service, how to refer a client to a doctor kindly, and how to fill in and protect the client record.

blocks.p: Every salon service starts with a consultation. In the ten minutes before you pick up a comb, you find out what the client wants, what her hair and scalp can take, and whether anything should stop you. A good consultation prevents damaged hair, burnt scalps, allergic reactions, spread infections and unhappy clients. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees and it sits under every other unit: shampooing, colouring, relaxing, thermal styling, braiding and wig work all begin here.

The unit title says 'diagnose', but a stylist does **not** diagnose disease. You learn to recognise the signs of common hair and scalp conditions, decide whether you can work, change the plan or must refer the client to a doctor, and explain that to her in plain, kind words. Only a doctor diagnoses and treats a medical condition.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the salon
rows: Prepare for and carry out a consultation
Seat the client at the work station, face to face, in good light and in private
Use open questions, listen, and watch her body language
Ask about hair care, chemical history, heat, styles, health, medicines and allergies
Explain the structure and growth of hair
Cuticle, cortex and medulla; follicle, bulb, papilla and sebaceous gland
Anagen, catagen and telogen, and normal daily shedding
Analyse the hair and scalp
Hair type and curl pattern, texture, density, porosity, elasticity and condition
The scalp, the hairline and the edges, checked section by section
Special care with natural, textured, relaxed and transitioning hair
Carry out hair and skin tests
Porosity, elasticity, pull and strand tests
Skin (patch) and incompatibility tests before chemical services, as the maker says
Recognise hair and scalp conditions
Tell infectious from non-infectious conditions
Know which ones stop the service and which only change it
Refer and advise
Describe what you see without naming a disease
Suggest a doctor or pharmacist, kindly and in private
Agree a plan and keep records
Agree the service, price, time and aftercare
Fill in the record card, have the client agree it, and keep it confidential
Work hygienically
Wash hands; clean and disinfect combs and clips; launder capes
Extra care after a client with lice or an infection

flow: Look at and feel the hair and scalp in sections
Decide: go ahead, change the plan, or refer
Explain in plain words and agree the service, price and aftercare
Fill in the record card and have the client agree it
Clean and disinfect; store the record safely

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the practicals you consult with a partner or model, carry out the tests, fill in a record card, make a conditions chart and act out referral role plays. The assessor marks your questions, your listening and your manner as much as your findings.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, scalp and record cards, never a client's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it. Never write a real client's name or health details on a role-play card.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Consult **before** the shampoo, with the hair dry. Wet hair hides its true colour, curl, shine and damage, and you cannot test porosity properly on wet hair.
Seat the client at the work station, face to face or through the mirror, in **good light** (daylight or bright white light, not a coloured bulb). A magnifying lamp helps you see the scalp.
Keep it **private**. Clients will not tell you about a scalp problem, a medicine or a home dye if the whole salon can hear. Lower your voice or move to a quieter spot.
Sit or stand at her level. Do not talk down to a client, and never lean over her from behind for the whole conversation.
Wash your hands before you touch her hair, and again after.

head: Type
Example
When to use it
rows: Open question
'Tell me about how you wash and style your hair at home.' 'What would you like to be different about your hair?'
At the start, to get the client talking and to learn things you did not think to ask.
Closed question
'Have you had a relaxer in the last six months?' 'Do you know of any allergies?'
To pin down a fact: a date, a product, a yes or no.
Leading question (avoid)
'You don't use heat every day, do you?'
It pushes the client to the answer you want, so you learn nothing. Ask it openly instead: 'How often do you use heat?'

blocks.h: What you need to find out

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she wants today, and how she wants her hair to look and feel afterwards
So the plan suits her, and so you can say early if it is not possible or not safe.
Home care: products, washing, combing, oils, grease, heat
Build-up, dryness, breakage and an oily or dry scalp often start at home.
Chemical history: relaxers, texturisers, colour, bleach, henna, home dyes, keratin and smoothing treatments, with dates
Chemicals weaken the hair and can react badly with each other. Metallic home dyes and compound henna can react with salon chemicals.
Styles worn: braids, cornrows, weaves, wigs, locs, tight ponytails, and for how long
Tight styles cause traction hair loss; braids and weaves hide the scalp and hold build-up.
Health: recent illness, high fever, surgery, pregnancy, thyroid or hormone problems, stress
They can cause heavy shedding or weak hair months later. Some mean a chemical service should wait.
Medicines and treatments
Some medicines thin the hair or make the scalp sensitive. The client need not name a condition; you only need to know whether her hair or skin may be affected.
Allergies and past reactions: colour, relaxer, adhesives, latex, nickel, fragrance
A past reaction means a skin test is essential, or the service may be ruled out.
Scalp problems now or before: itching, flaking, sores, pain, patches
They may be a contraindication, or a condition to work around.
Sun, sea and pool
In Jamaica, strong sun, sea water and chlorine dry the hair and fade colour.

ul: **Active listening**: look at her, nod, do not interrupt, and repeat back what you heard: 'So you had a relaxer in May and a semi-permanent colour last month. Is that right?'
Watch her **body language**. A frown, a flinch when you touch the hairline, or folded arms when you suggest a service all tell you something. Stop and ask gently.
Do not judge. A client who has been using a home relaxer kit or grease on her scalp needs advice, not a lecture.
Use plain words. Say 'the hair is very dry and breaks easily' rather than a long technical term, unless she asks.
If she speaks Patois, meet her where she is. Make sure she has understood the plan and the price before you start.

blocks.p: Everything a client tells you about her health, medicines, pregnancy or a scalp problem is **confidential**. Keep it between you, the client and the staff who need it to give the service. Record cards are kept in a locked drawer or a password-protected system, not on the reception desk or a phone's photo gallery. Never discuss a client's condition where others can hear, and never post it. Jamaica's data protection law gives clients the right to have their personal information kept safe and used only for the purpose it was collected for; a salon that leaks it loses trust and can be in trouble with the law.

blocks.note: Do not write 'has HIV' or 'taking tablets for her nerves' on a card. Record only what affects the service, for example 'medicine that may thin the hair: check with doctor before relaxer', and let the client see what you have written.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: How hair is built and how it grows

head: Part
What it is
Why it matters
rows: Follicle
A narrow pocket in the skin that the hair grows from. Its angle sets how straight or curly the hair is: a straight follicle gives straight hair, a strongly curved one gives coils.
Pulling on the follicle again and again (tight styles) can damage it for good.
Bulb
The rounded base of the hair root, inside the follicle.
Where the hair is made from living cells.
Dermal papilla
A small cone of tissue at the base of the bulb, full of tiny blood vessels.
It feeds the growing hair. Diet, illness and some medicines act on the hair through the blood supply here.
Sebaceous gland
An oil gland opening into the follicle, which makes sebum.
Sebum keeps the hair and scalp supple. Too much gives an oily scalp; too little gives a dry one.
Arrector pili muscle
A tiny muscle attached to the follicle.
It makes the hair stand up ('goose bumps').
Melanocytes
Cells in the bulb that make melanin, the hair's pigment.
Eumelanin gives brown and black; pheomelanin gives red and yellow. When they stop making pigment, the hair grows grey or white.

blocks.h: Above the skin: the hair shaft

head: Layer
What it is like
What it tells you
rows: Cuticle (outside)
Thin, clear, overlapping scales pointing towards the ends, like tiles on a roof. It has no colour of its own.
Flat and smooth: the hair shines, holds moisture, has low porosity. Raised, chipped or worn away: rough, dull, tangles, very porous, takes chemicals fast and unevenly.
Cortex (middle)
Bundles of keratin fibres held by bonds. It is most of the hair, and it holds the melanin.
Gives strength, stretch (elasticity) and natural colour. Relaxers, permanent colour and perms work here. Weak elasticity means a damaged cortex.
Medulla (centre)
A soft core of loose cells. Often missing in fine hair.
Little effect on salon services.

ul: **Hydrogen bonds**: weak, many, broken by water and heat and re-formed as the hair dries or cools. Wet sets and thermal styling use them. The change is temporary.
**Salt bonds**: broken by strong acids and alkalis. Also temporary.
**Disulphide bonds**: strong, fewer, between sulphur atoms in keratin. Only chemicals (relaxers, perms) change them, and the change is permanent.

head: Stage
What happens
Typical length
rows: Anagen
Active growth. New cells form in the bulb and push the hair up. Most of the hairs on a head (about 85 to 90 per cent) are in anagen.
Several years (often 2 to 7). The longer it lasts, the longer the hair can grow.
Catagen
A short change-over. Growth stops and the bulb shrinks away from the papilla.
A few weeks.
Telogen
Rest. The old hair sits loosely in the follicle until a new anagen hair pushes it out.
About 3 months. Roughly 10 per cent of hairs are resting at any time.

ul: Scalp hair grows about **1 to 1.5 cm a month**, a little faster in warm weather and in youth.
Because every follicle is at its own stage, losing **about 50 to 100 hairs a day** is normal. Hairs on the comb, the pillow and in the shower are telogen hairs being shed.

A shock to the body (high fever, surgery, childbirth, severe stress, crash dieting) can push many hairs into telogen at once. Two to three months later the client notices heavy shedding all over. This usually grows back, but the client should see a doctor if it is heavy or goes on.
As people age, anagen gets shorter and more follicles make grey hair.

blocks.note: When a client tells you she is 'going bald' because of hairs on her comb, ask how many, for how long, and whether she sees thin patches. A few dozen hairs a day with no patches is normal shedding. Hair in clumps, bald patches or a widening parting is not, and needs a doctor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: You analyse the hair by looking, feeling and testing, with the hair dry and clean of product where you can. Work in sections with a tail comb so that you see the whole head, not only the top. Write every finding on the record card as you go.

head: Type
What you see
What it means for services
rows: Straight (type 1)
No bend; often shiny and oily sooner, because sebum runs down easily.
Holds curl poorly; shows oil quickly.
Wavy (type 2)
Loose S-shapes.
Easily frizzed; needs light products.
Curly (type 3)
Springy curls or ringlets.
Drier; combs best when wet with conditioner.
Coily (type 4)
Tight coils or zig-zags; shrinks a lot as it dries (shrinkage), so it looks much shorter than it is.
Driest and most fragile: every bend is a weak point. Handle gently, in sections, with moisture. Judge true length by stretching a coil gently.

blocks.p: Most Jamaican clients have curly to coily hair, often with more than one pattern on the same head (looser at the nape or the crown, tighter at the edges). Note the patterns you find, and whether any part has lost its pattern (a sign of heat or chemical damage).

head: Characteristic
What it means
How to check
Results and what they tell you
rows: Texture
The thickness of one hair: fine, medium or coarse.
Roll a single hair between finger and thumb; compare with a hair you know. Fine hair is hard to feel; coarse hair feels like thread.
Fine hair is weak and processes fast; coarse hair is strong and resists chemicals and heat. Texture can differ round the head.
Density
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp: low, medium or high.
Part the hair in several places and see how much scalp shows.
High density needs more product and more sections. Low density shows thinning: compare the crown, the parting and the edges.
Porosity
How easily the hair takes in and loses moisture; it depends on the cuticle.
Slide a dry strand between finger and thumb from the ends towards the scalp. Or drop a clean hair into water and see how fast it sinks.

Smooth, slow to wet: low (tight cuticle; resists products). Slightly rough: normal. Rough, soaks water at once: high (raised or damaged cuticle; takes colour and relaxer fast and unevenly, loses moisture fast).
Elasticity
How far the hair stretches and returns without breaking: the health of the cortex.
Wet a single hair, hold both ends and stretch it gently.

Stretches about a third to a half and springs back: good. Snaps almost at once: dry and brittle, needs moisture. Stretches far, feels gummy and does not return: weak cortex, over-processed; needs protein and no chemicals for now.
Condition
The overall state: normal, dry, oily, damaged, chemically treated, heat-damaged.
Look at shine, ends, breakage, split ends, straight patches in curly hair; feel for roughness.
Decides whether you treat first, change the service or go ahead.
Length and growth
How much new growth since the last chemical service; how long the hair is.
Measure the new growth at the nape, the crown and the front with a ruler.
A retouch needs enough new growth; a client with 'no growth' may be breaking at the ends as fast as it grows.

ul: **Shrinkage** hides length and can hide breakage. Stretch a few coils gently to judge true length and look at the ends.
Coily hair is usually **dry** along the lengths even when the scalp is oily, because sebum cannot travel round the bends. Check porosity and elasticity at the ends, not only at the roots.
Look under braids, cornrows and weaves for build-up, flakes, soreness and thin spots, especially along the parts.
Check the **edges** and the nape. Short broken hairs, a receding hairline, small bumps or a smooth shiny area at the temples point to traction damage.

A **transitioning** client is growing out a relaxer. Where the natural new growth meets the relaxed hair is the **line of demarcation**. The two textures pull against each other there, so that is where the hair breaks. Advise gentle detangling, moisture, protective styles and regular trims of the relaxed ends, and no chemical over that line.
On locs, check for thinning at the root, build-up and mildew (a musty smell), and any locs that are too heavy for their root.

blocks.note: Many clients wear their hair under a wig, a scarf or in braids for weeks at a time. Always ask to see the natural hair and the scalp, and explain why: you cannot plan a service for hair you have not seen.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tests turn your opinion into evidence. Record every test with the date and the result, and keep the client's hair samples or strand-test notes where the Centre says. If the maker's instructions call for a test, it is not optional.

head: Test
How you do it
What it shows
When
rows: Porosity test
Dry hair: slide finger and thumb from the ends to the scalp. Or watch how quickly water soaks in.
How fast the hair will take in colour, relaxer and conditioner, and how fast it will lose moisture.
Every consultation; always before a chemical service.
Elasticity test
Stretch one wet hair gently between your fingers.
Strength of the cortex. Weak elasticity means no chemical service until the hair is treated.
Every consultation; always before a chemical service.
Pull test (traction test)
Take a small bunch of hair (about 50 hairs) between finger and thumb near the scalp and slide gently to the ends. Repeat in two or three places.
Whether hair is coming out more easily than normal. A few hairs (up to about five or six) is normal; more, or hairs with the bulb still attached in numbers, suggests active hair loss.
When the client complains of shedding or you see thinning.
Strand test (test curl / test cutting)
Apply the product to a small section or a few cut hairs, time it and watch, as the maker says.
How the hair reacts to a colour or relaxer, and how long it needs; whether it can take the service at all.
Before any chemical service, especially on porous, treated or unknown hair.
Skin test (patch test)

A little of the product, mixed if the maker says, on the skin behind the ear or inside the elbow; leave it uncovered for the time the maker says (often 48 hours) and check for redness, itching, swelling or blistering.
Whether the client is allergic to the product. A reaction means no service with that product.
Before colour, some relaxers and lace adhesives, as the maker says and as the Centre's rules say, usually 24 to 48 hours before.
Incompatibility test
Cut a few hairs, tie them, put them in a small dish of 20-volume hydrogen peroxide with a few drops of ammonia (or the maker's test mixture) and watch for up to 30 minutes.
Bubbling, heat, a bad smell or a colour change means metallic salts or another product in the hair that will react with the chemical service. Do not go ahead.
When the client has used a home dye, a 'progressive' grey cover or a compound henna, or cannot say what is on her hair.
Density and texture check
Parting the hair; rolling a single hair.
Thin, medium or thick; fine, medium or coarse.
Every consultation.

blocks.note: Pull gently in the pull test and the elasticity test. Stop if the client says it hurts, and never do a pull test on a sore or inflamed scalp. Wear gloves for the incompatibility test and keep the dish away from the client.
blocks.label: Safety

head: What the tests show
What you do
rows: Good elasticity, normal porosity, healthy scalp
Go ahead with the service, following the maker's instructions and your instructor.
High porosity, good elasticity
Go ahead with care: strand test, shorter timing on the porous parts, conditioning before and after.
Poor elasticity (snaps or stretches and stays)
No chemical service today. Give protein and moisture treatments over several weeks, trim damaged ends, and test again.
Positive skin test (red, itchy, swollen)
Do not use that product. Record it in bold on the card. Suggest a product without that ingredient only if the maker allows, with a new test.
Positive incompatibility test
No chemical service on that hair. Explain, record it, and plan a non-chemical service or wait until the treated hair is cut away.
Excess hairs in the pull test
Note it; do not do tight styles or harsh services; suggest a doctor if it goes on or there are patches.

blocks.p: Hair conditions are faults in the hair shaft or in its growth. None of them is infectious. Some you can treat in the salon with cutting and conditioning; some you must refer, because they are a sign of something happening in the body.

head: Condition
What you see
Usual cause
What the salon does
rows: Fragilitas crinium (split ends, brittle hair)
Ends split into two or more; hair feels rough and dry.
Dryness, heat, chemicals, rough combing, sun and sea.
Trim the splits (they travel up the hair if left); moisturising treatments; less heat; advise on protection.
Trichorrhexis nodosa (knotted hair)
Small white or swollen bumps along the hair, where it breaks like a frayed rope.
Harsh chemicals, hot tools, rough brushing, tight styling.
Cut away the damaged lengths; gentle handling; protein and moisture treatments; no chemicals until it improves.
Monilethrix (beaded hair)
Hair looks beaded, with thin and thick parts, and breaks short.
Inherited.
No chemicals or heat; very gentle care; refer the client to a doctor if she has not seen one.
Pili torti (twisted hair)
Hair flattened and twisted, dry, breaks easily.
Inherited, or sometimes from damage.
Gentle care, conditioning, no harsh services.
Canities (grey or white hair)
Hair with no pigment, often coarser and more resistant.
Age, inherited, sometimes stress or illness.
Colour services if the client wishes; grey hair may need a longer time or a different formula, as the maker says.
Hypertrichosis (hirsuties)
Excess hair on the face or body.
Hormones, inherited, some medicines.
Removal services in other units; refer if it starts suddenly.
Heat damage
Straight, limp pieces in curly hair that do not curl back after washing; dull, dry, rough; bubbles along the shaft (bubble hair) from irons on damp hair.
Too much heat, too often, on damp or unprotected hair.
Trim the damaged hair; treatments; rest from heat. The curl in the damaged part will not return.
Chemical damage (over-processing)
Gummy when wet, snaps when dry; limp; broken at one length (for example at the line of demarcation).
Overlapped relaxer, too long a timing, colour on top of relaxer too soon, bleaching.
Stop chemicals; protein then moisture treatments; trim; strand test before any future service.

head: Type
What you see
Cause
Salon action
rows: Traction alopecia
Thinning and short broken hairs along the hairline, temples, nape or along braid parts; sometimes small bumps; in the long run a smooth, shiny hairline where the follicles have died.
Tight braids, cornrows, weaves, wigs, ponytails and buns, and glued edges, over months and years.
Stop the pulling: looser styles, rest from braids and glue, no tension at the edges. Early traction loss grows back; long-term loss does not. Refer if it does not improve.
Alopecia areata
One or more round or oval, smooth, bald patches that appear suddenly; the skin looks normal.
The body's immune system attacks the follicles; often linked to stress or illness.
No chemicals or tight styles over the area; refer to a doctor. The hair often grows back, but treatment helps.
Alopecia totalis / universalis
Loss of all the scalp hair / all body hair.
As above, more severe.
Refer; wigs and scarves are a kind, practical help.
Androgenic (pattern) alopecia
Men: the hairline recedes at the temples and thins at the crown (male pattern baldness). Women: a widening parting and thinner hair on top, hairline usually kept.
Inherited and hormonal.
Styling to suit; no harsh services on thin areas; suggest a doctor if the client wants treatment.
Telogen effluvium (diffuse shedding)
Heavy shedding all over, 2 to 3 months after a shock to the body; the hair feels thinner but there are no bald patches.
Fever, illness, surgery, childbirth, crash dieting, severe stress, some medicines.
Reassure, gentle care, no tight styles; refer if it is heavy or lasts more than a few months.
Scarring (cicatricial) alopecia
A smooth, shiny, bald patch, often starting at the crown and spreading outwards; may be sore, itchy or have bumps. Common in women who have had many years of relaxers, heat and tight styles.
Inflammation that destroys the follicles.
Refer early: a doctor can stop it spreading, but lost follicles do not grow back. No chemicals or tension over the area.

blocks.note: Round, smooth patches that appeared suddenly, a crown that is thinning and sore, or hair coming out in clumps: these are not styling problems. Say what you see, kindly, and suggest a doctor (a dermatologist if she can). Do not promise that a treatment or product will grow the hair back.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The scalp is skin. It can be dry, oily, flaky, inflamed or infected like skin anywhere else. Your job is to spot the signs, decide whether the condition can be passed on, and decide whether you can work, must change the plan, or must refer. The rule is simple: **if it can spread, you do not work; if the skin is broken or inflamed, no chemicals and no heat over it.**

head: Condition
Signs
What the salon can do
rows: Pityriasis capitis (dry dandruff)
Small, dry, white or grey flakes that fall freely onto the shoulders; the scalp may itch; no redness.
Anti-dandruff shampoo as the maker says; regular shampooing; scalp massage; avoid heavy grease that traps the flakes. Not catching, but use clean tools as always.
Pityriasis steatoides (oily dandruff)
Larger, yellowish, greasy flakes stuck to the scalp; oily, often itchy, sometimes red.
Clarifying or medicated shampoo as the maker says; no heavy oils on the scalp. Refer if it is very red or weeping, because an infection can start in the broken skin.
Seborrhoea (oily scalp)
The scalp and roots are oily within a day or two of washing; hair looks lank; may have oily dandruff.
Balancing shampoo, a light massage (hard rubbing stimulates more oil), warm not hot water, light products.
Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Red, greasy, scaly patches on the scalp, hairline, eyebrows or behind the ears.
Mild products; no chemicals over inflamed skin; suggest a pharmacist or doctor.
Psoriasis
Thick, raised, red patches with silvery-white scales, often at the hairline, behind the ears and the nape; may bleed if scratched; not infectious.

Work gently around it with mild products if the skin is not broken; no chemicals, no heat and no friction on the patches; refer if it is sore or spreading. The client usually already knows she has it.
Eczema / contact dermatitis
Red, itchy, dry or weeping skin, sometimes where a product touched it (hairline, nape, ears).
Stop using the product that caused it; no chemicals on inflamed skin; refer if weeping or widespread.
Sebaceous cyst (wen, steatoma)
A soft, round, painless lump under the skin of the scalp, from a blocked oil gland.
Work around it gently; do not press, squeeze or comb over it. Refer if it is sore, growing or oozing.
Dry scalp
Tight, itchy scalp with fine flakes, often from hard water, hot water, harsh shampoo or dry weather.
Moisturising shampoo, cooler water, a light scalp oil, fewer washes.

head: Condition
Caused by
Signs
Why it matters
rows: Pediculosis capitis (head lice)
A parasite: a small grey-brown insect that lives on the scalp and feeds on blood.
Itching, especially at the nape and behind the ears; tiny oval eggs (nits) glued to the hairs close to the scalp that do not brush off; live lice; sometimes small red bites or scratch marks.
Spreads by head-to-head contact and through combs, towels, pillows and caps. No service; refer to a pharmacist or doctor; clean and disinfect everything the client touched.
Tinea capitis (ringworm of the scalp)
A fungus.
Round or oval, scaly, itchy patches; hairs broken off short so the patch looks stubbly or bald; sometimes a raised ring with a clearer centre; can become a boggy, pus-filled swelling (kerion).
Spreads by contact and through tools, towels and head rests. No service; refer to a doctor, who gives tablets. Common in children.
Impetigo
Bacteria.
Small blisters or sores that burst and dry into yellow, honey-coloured crusts, often round the mouth, nose, hairline and scalp; itchy.
Very contagious by touch. No service; refer to a doctor.
Folliculitis
Bacteria in the follicles (sometimes from dirty tools or shaving).
Small red, pus-filled spots at the base of the hairs; sore; may crust.
Can spread. No service on the area; refer if there are many spots or they keep returning. Sycosis barbae is folliculitis of the beard.
Boils (furuncles)
A deep bacterial infection of a follicle.
A large, painful, red swelling with a yellow head, often at the nape.
No service near it; refer.
Scabies
A mite that burrows into the skin.
Intense itching, worse at night; fine lines and bumps between the fingers, at the wrists, elbows and waist; rarely the scalp in adults.
Spreads by close contact. No service; refer.
Warts (verrucae)
A virus.
Small, rough, raised growths on the skin.
Avoid cutting or combing over them; they can spread by contact.

blocks.h: What to do when you find a contagious condition

flow: Stop touching the hair; put down the comb
Describe what you see, in plain words, without naming a disease as fact
Explain that you cannot carry on today, and why: it could spread or get worse
Suggest a pharmacist or doctor and offer to rebook when it has cleared
Record what you saw and advised
Bag the cape and towels for a hot wash; clean, then disinfect the comb, clips and chair; wash your hands

blocks.p: Say, for example: 'Miss Brown, I can see some small eggs stuck on the hair at the back of Kaylia's neck. I can't do the plaits today, because it could spread to the other children here. The pharmacist on the main road can give you something, and I'll keep the Saturday slot for you when it's clear.' That is honest, kind and private, and it is not a diagnosis.

blocks.note: Never say 'she has ringworm' or 'you have lice' as a fact, and never say it in front of other clients. You describe; the doctor diagnoses. If you are not sure whether a patch is ringworm or psoriasis, treat it as if it could spread and refer.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: After a client with lice or a fungal infection: combs and clips are washed in hot soapy water, then put in disinfectant for the full contact time. Capes and towels go straight into a sealed bag and a hot wash. Wipe the chair, head rest and trolley with disinfectant. Lice cannot live long off the head, but eggs and fungal spores can wait on tools.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Factors that affect hair, choosing the service, and records

head: Factor
Effect on the hair and scalp
What you look or ask for
rows: Heredity
Texture, density, curl pattern, early greying and pattern hair loss run in families.
'Does anyone in your family have thin hair or early grey?'
Diet and water
Hair is made of protein. Too little protein, iron, zinc or water gives thin, dull, slow-growing hair.
Dull, weak hair with no other cause.
Health, hormones and medicines
Fever, surgery, thyroid problems, pregnancy and childbirth, anaemia, stress and some medicines (for blood pressure, acne, cancer and others) cause shedding or weak hair.
Heavy shedding, a change the client noticed over months.
Age
Growth slows, hair thins, greys, and becomes drier.
Plan gentler services and adjust timings as the maker says.
Chemical services
Relaxers, perms, colour and bleach weaken the cortex and raise the cuticle, especially if overlapped or done too often.
Dates, products, who did them, any reactions.
Heat
Blow-dryers, flat irons, pressing combs and curling irons dry the hair, raise the cuticle and can cook the cortex.
How often, how hot, with or without protectant.
Styling tension
Tight braids, weaves, wigs, ponytails and glued edges pull on the follicles.
How long styles are kept in, how tight, where it hurts.
Home products
Build-up from heavy grease, gels and waxes; harsh shampoos that strip; home dyes with metallic salts.
What she uses and how often; anything that could react with a chemical service.
Climate and water
Jamaica's sun, sea water, sweat and humidity dry the hair, fade colour and make pressed hair revert; hard water leaves a dulling film.
Outdoor work, sea bathing, swimming pools, the water at home.

head: Finding
Decision
rows: Healthy hair and scalp, tests good
Go ahead with the service she wants, within the maker's instructions.
Dry, porous but strong hair
Go ahead with care: treatment first or after, shorter timing, strand test.
Weak elasticity, breakage, over-processed
Postpone chemicals and heat. Offer treatments, a trim and a protective style. Rebook and test again.
Traction damage at the edges
No tension on the edges, no glue, looser styles; a break from braids and weaves.
Non-infectious scalp condition with unbroken skin
Go ahead gently with mild products; nothing harsh over the area.
Broken, inflamed or weeping skin
No chemicals, no heat, no friction. Shampoo only if it will not hurt, or refer.
Signs of a contagious condition
No service. Refer. Clean and disinfect.
Positive skin or incompatibility test
No chemical service with that product on that hair.

blocks.p: Then **agree** the plan: what you will do today, what it will cost, how long it takes, what the result will look like and what she must do at home. If you cannot give her what she asked for, say so clearly and offer what you can. A client who hears 'not today, and here is why, and here is what we can do instead' comes back; a client whose hair breaks does not.

head: Part of the card
What goes in it
rows: Client details
Name, phone number, date of first visit; the stylist's name.
History
Health points that affect the service, allergies and past reactions, medicines that affect hair or skin (in general terms), chemical services with dates and products, styles worn, home care.
Analysis
Hair type and curl pattern, texture, density, porosity, elasticity, condition, length and new growth, scalp condition, edges.
Tests
Each test, the date, the product and the result; the date a skin test was done and whether it was clear.
Plan and service
The service agreed, the product, strength, timing, result, price, and anything that went wrong.
Advice and referral
Aftercare and products advised; whether you referred her and why; what she was told.
Agreement
The client's signature or agreement that her answers are true and she agrees to the plan.

ul: Write it **during** the consultation, not from memory at the end of the day.
Write clearly in ink. A card that another stylist cannot read is useless.
Update it at every visit. A test result from last year does not cover a service today.
Keep cards **locked away** and digital records password-protected. Only staff who need them see them.
If there is ever a complaint or a reaction, the record card shows what was asked, tested, agreed and done.

blocks.note: Record cards are evidence for the client, the stylist and the salon. The client knows her allergies are on file; the next stylist knows what the hair has had; the salon can show that it tested and advised properly. Keep them for the time the Centre or the salon's rules say.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: I can set up a consultation in good light and in private, and explain why it is done on dry hair before the shampoo.
I can ask open questions, listen actively, repeat back, and read a client's body language.
I can list what to ask about: home care, chemical history, styles, health, medicines, allergies, scalp problems, sun and sea.
I can name the parts of the hair root and the three layers of the shaft, and say what the cuticle and cortex do.
I can describe anagen, catagen and telogen, say how much daily shedding is normal, and recognise shedding that needs a doctor.
I can check and record hair type and curl pattern, texture, density, porosity, elasticity and condition.
I can analyse natural, coily, braided, loc'd and transitioning hair, and find the line of demarcation and traction damage.
I can carry out and read porosity, elasticity, pull, strand, skin and incompatibility tests, and say when each is needed.
I can recognise split ends, trichorrhexis nodosa, monilethrix, canities, heat and chemical damage, and say what the salon can do.
I can recognise traction, areata, pattern, diffuse and scarring hair loss, and say which need a doctor.
I can recognise dandruff, seborrhoea, psoriasis, eczema and a sebaceous cyst, and work safely around them.
I can recognise head lice, ringworm, impetigo, folliculitis and scabies, and say why the service must stop.
I can refer a client kindly, in private, describing what I see without naming a disease.
I can clean and disinfect tools and launder capes after a contagious condition.
I can explain how diet, health, medicines, chemicals, heat, tension, home products and Jamaica's climate affect the hair.
I can decide whether to go ahead, change the plan or refer, and agree a service, price and aftercare.
I can fill in a record card fully, have the client agree it, and keep it confidential.

blocks.note: In the essay paper, give the sign, then the action, then the reason. 'Round scaly patches with broken hairs: I stop, explain privately and suggest a doctor, because ringworm is a fungus that spreads through tools and touch.' Three parts, every time.
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The talk and examination before a service, to find out what the client wants and what her hair and scalp can safely take.
A question that cannot be answered with yes or no, so the client tells you more.
Keeping a client's personal and health information private and secure.
A sign or condition that means a service should not be done, or should be changed.
Advising a client to see a doctor or pharmacist about a condition you have noticed.
The pocket in the skin that a hair grows from.
The tissue at the base of the bulb that feeds the growing hair.
The oil gland attached to the follicle that makes sebum.
The outer layer of overlapping scales on the hair shaft.
The middle layer of the hair, which gives strength, elasticity and colour.
The soft centre of the hair, often missing in fine hair.
The pigment that gives hair its colour: eumelanin (brown-black) and pheomelanin (red-yellow).
The growing, change-over and resting stages of the hair growth cycle.
The thickness of a single hair: fine, medium or coarse.
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp: low, medium or high.
How easily the hair takes in and loses moisture; set by the state of the cuticle.
How far the hair stretches and returns without breaking; a sign of the cortex's health.
The way coily hair draws up and looks shorter as it dries.
The point where natural new growth meets chemically treated hair; the weakest point on the strand.
Gently drawing a small bunch of hair to see whether more than a few hairs come out.
Testing a product on a small section or cut hairs to see how the hair reacts and how long it needs.
A small amount of product on the skin, left for the maker's time, to check for allergy.
A test on cut hairs for metallic salts or other products that would react with a chemical service.
Knotted or swollen points along the hair where it frays and breaks.
Beaded hair that breaks easily; inherited.
Hair loss. Traction (from pulling), areata (sudden round patches), androgenic (pattern), scarring (follicles destroyed).
Heavy shedding all over, a few months after illness, childbirth or stress.
Dry dandruff; pityriasis steatoides is the oily, greasy kind.
Thick, red patches with silvery scales; not infectious.
A soft lump under the skin from a blocked oil gland.
Head lice; the eggs are nits.
Ringworm of the scalp, a fungal infection; round scaly patches with broken hairs.
A bacterial skin infection with weeping sores and honey-coloured crusts.
Infection of the hair follicles: small red spots with pus.
The client's written record of history, analysis, tests, services, advice and agreement.

c1.title: Edges and a relaxer before a wedding in Portmore
c1.text: Shanique Grant, 29, comes to a salon in Portmore three weeks before her sister's wedding. She wants a relaxer today so that her hair will 'lie flat' under the bridesmaid's headpiece. She has worn sew-in weaves back to back for two years, and her last relaxer was about ten months ago, before the weaves. When trainee Abigail parts the hair at the front, the hairline is thin, with short broken hairs and a few small bumps at the temples, and Shanique winces when the comb touches it. The rest of the hair is coily, dry and about 8 cm long with relaxed ends. Abigail is working at the reception desk, where two other clients are waiting.

c2.title: A scaly patch on a schoolboy in Brown's Town
c2.text: Mr. Dwight Palmer brings his son Javon, 7, to a barber-and-beauty salon in Brown's Town for a trim before the new term. Javon has been scratching one spot for about two weeks. Trainee Keneisha sees a round, scaly, greyish patch about 3 cm across on the crown. The hairs inside it are broken off close to the skin, so the patch looks stubbly, and the edge is slightly raised. There is no pus or honey-coloured crust. Two other children are waiting for cuts.

c3.title: Transitioning hair in Half-Way-Tree
c3.text: Rochelle Daley, 24, a bank clerk, visits a salon in Half-Way-Tree. She stopped relaxing seven months ago and has about 5 cm of natural new growth under relaxed ends that reach her shoulders. She combs the hair dry from the roots every morning and uses a flat iron twice a week 'to blend the two textures'. She complains that her hair is 'not growing': hair is all over the bathroom floor, but it is in short pieces, not full-length strands. Trainee Marsha tests a wet hair from the relaxed length: it stretches a long way, feels gummy and does not spring back. A dry strand from the natural part feels rough from end to root.

c4.title: Sudden patches on a fisherman in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: Mr. Linton Reid, 52, a fisherman from Savanna-la-Mar, comes in for his usual low cut. The trainee, Omar, notices two smooth, round, completely bald patches about the size of a J$ 20 coin on the back of the head. The skin inside them looks normal: no scales, no redness, no broken hairs. Mr. Reid says they 'just appeared' over the last month, around the time his boat engine was stolen. He also asks whether the grey coming in at his temples means his hair is 'dying', and mentions that his father and brothers all went bald at the crown by fifty.

c5.title: Flakes, oil and a home dye in Morant Bay
c5.text: Mrs. Yvonne Francis, 46, a market vendor from Morant Bay, books a shampoo and a permanent colour to cover her grey. Her scalp is oily two days after washing, with large, yellowish, greasy flakes stuck along the parting, and it itches. Behind her left ear is a thick, raised, red patch with silvery-white scales that she says she has had 'on and off for years'. She has been using a 'progressive' grey-cover lotion from a shop, a little each week, for the last three months. The trainee, Danielle, has to decide what to test and whether the colour can go ahead.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the thin, broken hairline and the bumps at Shanique's temples?
o: Alopecia areata brought on by stress about the wedding
Ringworm of the scalp caught from a shared comb
Traction from two years of tight sew-in weaves
Over-processing from her relaxer ten months ago
questions.why: Thinning, short broken hairs and small bumps along the hairline after years of weaves are the classic signs of traction alopecia. Areata gives smooth round patches, ringworm gives scaly patches with broken hairs, and the relaxer was long before the weaves.

questions.q: Abigail is consulting at the reception desk with other clients listening. What should she do first?
o: Move her to the work station, where the talk can be private
Carry on at the desk, because the questions are only about hair
Finish quickly so the waiting clients are not held up
Ask the waiting clients to step outside for a few minutes
questions.why: A consultation covers health, medicines and scalp problems, which are confidential. It belongs at the work station, in good light and out of earshot. The waiting clients should not be sent out, and rushing misses facts.

questions.q: Which is the best plan to agree with Shanique for the wedding?
o: Relax today but keep the relaxer off the front 2 cm of hairline
A mild relaxer today, then a deep conditioning treatment
A texturiser, because it is gentler on the edges than a relaxer
A low-tension protective style and treatments, no relaxer now
questions.why: Her edges are damaged and sore, and the hair is dry with old relaxed ends, so a chemical service now risks more breakage and a burn on the tender hairline. Rest for the edges, moisture and a style with no pull is the safe plan, and the headpiece can be worked around it.

questions.q: Shanique says she did not know weaves could do this and looks upset. What is the best way for Abigail to explain?
o: Warn her that the hairline is badly damaged and will probably never grow back
Show her the thin area and explain that pulling caused it and rest will help
Say that the people who did the weaves were careless and she should change salons
Tell her it is nothing to worry about and that edge-control gel will hide it
questions.why: A good explanation is honest, plain and kind: it shows the client what you see, names the cause without blaming anyone, and gives a hopeful but truthful next step. Frightening her or hiding the problem both fail her.

questions.q: What do the signs on Javon's crown most suggest?
o: Psoriasis, because the patch is scaly and raised
Tinea capitis, a fungal infection of the scalp
Dry dandruff from a scalp that is not washed often
Impetigo, because the spot is itchy and crusted
questions.why: A round, scaly patch with hairs broken off short and a slightly raised edge is the picture of scalp ringworm, which is common in children. Psoriasis has silvery scales on unbroken hair, dandruff has no bald patch, and impetigo has weeping sores with honey crusts.

questions.q: What should Keneisha do about the trim?
o: Trim the rest of the head but keep the clippers away from the patch
Trim as booked, then disinfect the clippers for twice the usual time
Put a dab of antiseptic on the patch, wait ten minutes, then trim
Not cut today; speak to Mr. Palmer privately and suggest a doctor
questions.why: A fungal infection spreads through tools and touch, so no service is given until a doctor has treated it. The stylist describes what she sees, refers, and rebooks; she does not treat it herself.

questions.q: Mr. Palmer asks, 'Is it ringworm?' Which reply is right for a trainee?
o: 'I can't name it, but I can see a scaly patch, and a doctor should check it.'
'Yes, it is ringworm, and the pharmacy sells a cream you can put on it.'
'No, it's just dry scalp, but see a doctor anyway to be safe.'
'It looks like ringworm or psoriasis, so try a dandruff shampoo for a week first.'
questions.why: A stylist describes what she sees and refers; only a doctor diagnoses and prescribes. The second answer is honest, kind and clear about the next step without naming a disease as fact or guessing at a treatment.

questions.q: After the Palmers leave, what must happen to the comb, the neck strip and the cape that touched Javon's head?
o: Rinse the comb under the tap and use the UV cabinet; bin the neck strip; air the cape
Spray the comb, neck strip and cape with disinfectant and leave them on the trolley
Wash and then disinfect the comb; bin the neck strip; bag the cape for a hot wash
Wipe the comb and cape with a towel and reuse them, since fungus cannot live on plastic
questions.why: Fungal spores survive on tools and fabric. Tools are cleaned and then disinfected for the full time, single-use items are thrown away, and fabrics are laundered hot. A UV cabinet and spraying do not disinfect dirty items.

questions.q: What do Marsha's two tests show about Rochelle's hair?
o: The relaxed length lacks moisture; the natural hair has low porosity
The relaxed length has good elasticity; the natural hair is normal
The relaxed length is heat damaged; the natural hair has good elasticity
Relaxed length weak from over-processing; natural hair highly porous
questions.why: Hair that stretches far, feels gummy and does not return has a weak cortex from chemical over-processing. A strand that feels rough all the way to the root has a raised cuticle, which is high porosity.

questions.q: Why is Rochelle finding short pieces of hair rather than whole strands?
o: Her hair is in telogen and the pieces are the shed ends
The hair is breaking, most likely where the textures meet
Her flat iron is cutting the hair as it slides through
Short pieces like this are normal shedding for natural hair
questions.why: Shed hairs are full length with a bulb at the root. Short pieces mean breakage, and in transitioning hair the weakest point is where the two textures meet, made worse by dry combing from the roots and twice-weekly heat.

questions.q: Which advice should Marsha give Rochelle to keep the length she grows?
o: Relax the new growth so both textures match and stop pulling against each other
Flat iron more often at a higher heat so the textures blend and tangle less
Detangle wet from the ends, trim relaxed ends over time, use little heat
Comb the hair dry every morning with a fine-tooth comb to stop knots forming
questions.why: Transitioning hair survives by gentle handling: detangling from the ends on wet, conditioned hair, trimming the weak relaxed ends gradually, protective styles and little heat. Relaxing again ends the transition, and dry combing and more heat cause the breakage she already has.

questions.q: What should Marsha write on Rochelle's record card about the tests?
o: 'Elasticity poor (relaxed hair), porosity high (natural hair)', date, advice
'Hair in bad condition' and the date, with a note to see her again
Only the advice she was given, because the tests showed nothing that needed recording
The brand of relaxer she used to use and the month she stopped using it
questions.why: A record card holds each test, its result and the date, plus the plan and advice, so that the next stylist knows what the hair was like and what was agreed. Vague notes and missing results are of no use later.

questions.q: What do the smooth, round, bald patches on Mr. Reid's head most suggest, and what should Omar do?
o: Alopecia areata; cut round the patches and suggest a doctor
Male pattern baldness; advise him to keep the cut low
Ringworm; stop the cut and disinfect the clippers
Traction alopecia; advise a looser hat and fewer low cuts in future
questions.why: Sudden, smooth, round bald patches with normal skin and no scaling point to alopecia areata, which is not infectious but needs a doctor. Pattern baldness is gradual at the temples and crown, ringworm is scaly with broken hairs, and traction loss follows the hairline.

questions.q: Mr. Reid asks whether his new grey hair means his hair is dying. What is the correct explanation?
o: Grey hair is dead hair that no longer grows from the root and will fall out
Salt in sea water has bleached the cortex, which is why it turns grey early
The bulb has stopped making melanin, so the hair grows without colour
The grey is the first stage of the pattern baldness that runs in his family
questions.why: Canities is hair that grows without pigment because the melanocytes in the bulb have stopped making melanin. It is normal with age and heredity; the hair is alive, and greying is not a stage of pattern baldness.

questions.q: If Mr. Reid later develops a receding hairline at the temples and thinning at the crown, like his father and brothers, which condition is this?
o: Telogen effluvium
Androgenic alopecia
Alopecia totalis
Cicatricial alopecia
questions.why: Hair loss at the temples and crown that runs in the family is androgenic, or male pattern, alopecia. Telogen effluvium is diffuse shedding after a shock, totalis is loss of all scalp hair, and scarring alopecia destroys the follicles with inflammation.

questions.q: Which scalp condition do the greasy, yellowish flakes stuck along Mrs. Francis's parting suggest?
o: Dry dandruff, pityriasis capitis, with small white flakes
Folliculitis, an infection of the follicles with pus spots
Head lice, pediculosis capitis, with nits on the hair
Oily dandruff, pityriasis steatoides, on an oily scalp
questions.why: Large, greasy, yellowish flakes stuck to an oily, itchy scalp are oily dandruff on an over-oily scalp. Dry dandruff is small, white and falls freely; folliculitis shows pus-filled spots; lice show nits glued to the hairs.

questions.q: What is the thick, raised, red patch with silvery scales behind her ear most likely to be, and does it stop the colour service?
o: Impetigo; yes, it is contagious and the colour must wait
Psoriasis; not contagious, but no colour on the patch
Tinea capitis; yes, it is contagious and the colour must wait
Seborrhoea; no, the colour can go on as normal over the patch
questions.why: Thick red plaques with silvery-white scales that come and go for years are typical of psoriasis. It cannot be passed on, but colour must not go on inflamed or broken skin, and a sore patch should be seen by a doctor.

questions.q: Because of the grey-cover lotion, which test must Danielle do before any permanent colour, and what does a positive result look like?
o: An incompatibility test; cut hairs bubble or change colour
A pull test; more than a few hairs come out in her hand
A skin test; the skin goes red and itchy within 48 hours
An elasticity test; the hair stretches a long way and stays
questions.why: Progressive grey-cover lotions often contain metallic salts, which react with the peroxide in permanent colour. Cut hairs are tested in peroxide with a little ammonia; bubbling, heat, a smell or discolouring means the colour cannot go ahead on that hair.

questions.q: The test on Mrs. Francis's cut hairs fizzes and warms within a few minutes. What should Danielle do?
o: Go ahead with the colour, but halve the processing time to be safe
Shampoo twice with a clarifying shampoo to remove the lotion, then colour
Use a semi-permanent colour instead, because it has no developer in it
Not colour it; explain why, record it and offer a non-chemical service
questions.why: A positive incompatibility test means the hair could overheat, break or discolour under a chemical service. Clarifying does not remove metallic salts from inside the hair. The treated hair must grow out or be cut before an oxidative colour is used.

questions.q: A client, Mrs. Hyde, tells a trainee in confidence that she is on a medicine that thins her hair. Later the trainee's friend, who also uses the salon, asks why Mrs. Hyde's hair looks so thin. What should the trainee do?
o: Explain that it is the medicine, since the friend is also a client
Tell the friend to ask Mrs. Hyde herself, and hint that it is medical
Say only that she cannot discuss another client's details
Describe the hair loss but not the medicine's name
questions.why: Health details given in a consultation are confidential. They are shared only with staff who need them for the service, never with other clients, friends or online, and hinting is still a breach of trust.
